title: Ang 1231: the ninth Guru in Sarang
tomorrow: why would a Guru need a longer hymn to say it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjan's Sarang: in the hottest hour, the Name runs cool. Now the headings jump again, from Mahala 5 to Mahala 9, and the ninth Guru asks a hard question.
screen: `ARJAN'S SARANG: THE NAME RUNS COOL.` → `MAHALA 9 AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Every form wants an emergency contact. One name, one number: the person who'll come. On ang 1231, in Sarang, Guru Tegh Bahadur writes a line that seems to cross the whole list out. In paraphrase: without the Lord, no one is your helper. Whose mother, whose father, whose son, whose wife? Who is anyone's brother? It sounds cold the first time. So why would a Guru ask it?
screen: `ONE NAME, ONE NUMBER.` → `WHOSE MOTHER, WHOSE FATHER?` → `WHY WOULD A GURU ASK?`

segments.voice: The question underneath is old: who, in the end, can hold you? The ninth Guru's answer is honest about people. Mother, father, child, spouse, brother: real ties, loved ties, and every one of them can move away, get sick, run out of strength, or simply not be able to reach where you are. The hymn doesn't say they don't matter. Sikh teaching honors family life. It says they aren't the final helper. That's the Lord, and the hymn turns the listener to the Name while there's time. A neighbor tradition pictures something close. In the Qur'an, Surah 80, in paraphrase: on that day a person will flee from their brother, and their mother and father, and their spouse and children; each will have enough concern of their own. The shared part is real. Both look straight at the people we lean on most and admit there's a place they can't come with us. Both turn toward God there. The difference is real too. The Qur'an sets that scene on the Day of Judgment, each soul answering for itself, hoping in God's mercy. The ninth Guru speaks of now, of this life, and of attachment, and points to the Name as the helper today. Two neighbors, standing at the same edge, describing it in their own words.
screen: `WHO CAN HOLD YOU, IN THE END?` · `REAL TIES, NOT THE FINAL HELPER.` · `SURAH 80: ON THAT DAY.` · `THE NINTH GURU: NOW, AND THE NAME.` · then, large: `THE NINTH.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers the people who've helped you this year, one name per finger. Thank each one silently, and let them go, the way you'd set down something precious, gently. Then rest in what's left when the list is done. If you'd like, read ang 1231 before you begin.
Ang 1231. Where Guru Tegh Bahadur, in Sarang, asks whose mother and whose father, and names the Lord as the helper.
The ninth, again: love your people, and know they aren't the last helper. The Name is. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: a friend moving across the country quotes the ninth Guru: "whose mother, whose father?" and says, "so I shouldn't miss anyone." what's the fair reading?
options: miss them; the ties are real. the hymn just says they aren't the final helper.
right: the hymn says loving family is a mistake.
the hymn is only about death, so moving has nothing to do with it.
fork.reveal: the hymn doesn't cancel love. it admits every human helper has limits and points to the Lord, and the Name, as the one who doesn't.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sahaaee, helper. the hymn says without the Lord, no one is your helper.

chat.says: a kid asked if i'll be his counselor next year. i'm leaving for college. he looked crushed
options: be honest: you won't be here. tell him people move, and he's still held.
say maybe next year, so he doesn't have to be sad about it yet.
tell him people don't really matter in the end; only God does.
chat.meaning: The ninth Guru's hymn admits human ties move and have limits, without saying they don't matter, and points to the Lord as the helper who stays.
